metadata.title: How Do You Actually Know It Worked?

beats.narration_text: Hi — I'm Divij Pawar. Last time, we ended on an uncomfortable fact: an agent that's stuck can look identical to one that succeeded, right up until someone checks. Today: three real mechanisms that turn 'the agent says it worked' into something you can actually stand behind — and exactly where they stop working.

props.command: How do you actually know an AI agent's reasoning is trustworthy?
props.segment: How Do You Know It Worked?
output: Extraction: turn reasoning into checkable claims, not a story
Verification: fetch the real source, check the number matches
Consistency: run it twice, see if the numbers survive

beats.narration_text: Here's the uncomfortable starting point. When an agent explains its reasoning — 'I checked the numbers, cross-referenced the filing, and concluded X' — that explanation was generated by the same model that generated the conclusion. It's not a transcript of what happened. It's a plausible-sounding narration, produced after the fact. A model that hallucinated a number can write a perfectly coherent paragraph about how it derived that number. Fluency and accuracy are different properties, and a language model optimizes hard for the first one. The real question isn't whether the explanation sounds reasonable — it's whether any part of it can be checked against something outside the model itself. The log is evidence of output. It is not evidence of process.

shot.visual_intent: The executive-summary beat — states the whole episode's thesis before any mechanism is introduced. A split screen contrasts a mostly-blank 'What Actually Happened' box against a confident, fully-written 'What the Model Says Happened' box, joined by a dotted line the narration then challenges.

show.event: Title 'The Trust Problem' writes on
A vertical divider draws; left box labeled 'What Actually Happened' seats mostly empty/ghost; right box labeled 'What the Model Says Happened' seats full of confident text lines
A dotted line draws connecting the two boxes, captioned 'assumed to be the same thing'
One of the right box's confident lines gets a question mark beside it as 'fluency and accuracy are different properties' lands beneath
Both boxes and the dotted line fade
A serif landing line holds center: 'The log is evidence of output — not evidence of process.'

beats.narration_text: The first move is to stop treating the reasoning as one continuous story, and start treating it as a pile of individual, checkable assertions. Run the text through a parser that pulls out four kinds of claims: citations, wherever the text points to a source; quantitative claims — dollar figures, percentages, multiples, basis points; hedge language — words like 'approximately' or 'assumed', flagging the model's own uncertainty; and causal claims — sentences using 'because' or 'resulting in', where the model asserts one thing caused another. Take a real line: 'Revenue grew 34 percent year over year, driven by international expansion — source: the 10-K.' The parser tags it three ways at once: quantitative, causal, and citation. None of this requires understanding what the text means. It's pattern matching — regular expressions hunting for percent signs, source brackets, and a fixed list of hedge words. You're not asking a second AI to judge the reasoning. You're mechanically converting prose into a checklist of falsifiable pieces.

shot.visual_intent: A wall of prose runs through a shredder-like animation and comes out as four labeled cards (CITATION / QUANTITATIVE / HEDGE / CAUSAL) — the real four claim types from this project's own claims.py. A single worked example line then gets tagged live, threading through the rest of the mechanism beats.

show.event: Title 'Claim Extraction' writes on
A block of dense paragraph lines (dummy prose) fades in center
The paragraph block runs through a shredder shape and re-emerges as four cards: CITATION, QUANTITATIVE, HEDGE, CAUSAL
A real code caption seats beneath the cards: 'ClaimType: citation | quantitative | hedge | causal'

The worked-example line fades in: 'Revenue grew 34% YoY, driven by international expansion — source: 10-K', with the '34%' phrase underlined in the QUANTITATIVE accent, 'driven by' in the CAUSAL accent, and 'source: 10-K' in the CITATION accent
A hedge-word row fades in beneath: 'approximately · unclear · assumed'
Caption lands: 'no second AI — just pattern matching'
A serif landing line holds: 'prose becomes a checklist of falsifiable pieces'

beats.narration_text: Extraction gives you a list of claims. It doesn't tell you if any of them are true — that's the next step, and it actually leaves the model's head entirely. Take that citation — 'source: the 10-K' — and the system fetches it for real. If it's a government filing, it parses the structured data directly: real reported numbers, not text scraped off a page. Otherwise, it searches the raw text for numbers. Then it checks: does a matching number show up in that source, within about one percent, to allow for rounding? A citation lands in one of three states: the source is reachable and a number matches; the source is reachable and nothing matches — a real red flag; or the fetch itself fails — unattainable, no judgment possible either way.

shot.visual_intent: The CITATION card fetches a real source. Real on-screen artifact: this project's actual tristate (verified: bool | None) and its actual 1% tolerance function, shown as real code rather than an invented three-label enum (see SOURCES.md correction).

show.event: Title 'Verify Against Reality' writes on
The CITATION card from B02 floats up-left; an arrow shoots toward a small filing-document icon on the right
The document icon splits into two branches: 'government filing → structured data' and 'generic page → raw text search'
A real code line seats beneath: '_close_enough(a, b, tol=0.01)  # within ~1%'
Three outcome chips fade in left to right: 'reachable, number matches', 'reachable, nothing matches', 'fetch failed — unattainable'
The middle chip ('nothing matches') pulses in the accent color, captioned 'a real red flag'
The third chip is captioned 'no judgment possible either way'
A serif landing line holds: 'an honest system can say: I don't know'

beats.narration_text: Roll all of that up into one number — the fraction of citations actually confirmed — and a human reviewer has something to act on that has nothing to do with how convincing the writing sounds. Say our 34 percent claim checks out against the real filing; across a whole reasoning trace, that might land at six of nine citations confirmed — sixty-seven percent. One honest caveat: the check isn't perfectly tight. It pools every number in the whole reasoning trace and asks whether any of them shows up in the source — so a citation can get marked confirmed on the strength of a completely unrelated number. That's a real gap, not a rounding error, and it's worth knowing before you trust the number too much.

shot.visual_intent: The worked example resolves (34% confirmed against the filing), rolling up into a single verification-rate number — then an honest caveat card about the real pooling behavior in this project's own verification.py, so the mechanism isn't oversold.

show.event: Title 'The Verification Rate' writes on
The worked example's '34%' chip gets a checkmark against a small filing icon
A percentage counter ticks up center: '6 of 9 citations confirmed — 67%'
A caption card slides in beneath, bordered in the accent: 'checks whether ANY number in the trace matches ANY number in the source'
Caption continues: 'a real gap, not a rounding error'
A serif landing line holds: 'a number a human reviewer can actually act on'

beats.act: mechanism 3 — ask the same question twice
beats.narration_text: Verification catches claims that point at real sources. But plenty of reasoning doesn't cite anything external at all — it's synthesis, judgment, 'based on everything above, I conclude X.' You can't fetch a source for that. So you use a different trick: ask the same question twice. Run the identical query through the full reasoning process a second time, completely independently. Then compare the two conclusions — how much do the actual words overlap, and, weighted more heavily, how much do the specific numbers overlap. A model reasoning from real evidence should land in roughly the same place twice. A model confabulating a plausible story tends to drift, especially on the numbers, because a fabricated number is much harder to reproduce identically than a fabricated vibe.

shot.visual_intent: The identical query runs through two parallel agent boxes; a comparison meter shows the real word/number weighting from this project's consistency.py (0.4 words, 0.6 numbers).

show.event: Title 'Ask The Same Question Twice' writes on
One input box duplicates into two identical copies, each feeding a separate 'Agent' box below it
Two conclusion output boxes emerge beneath the agent boxes
A comparison meter seats between them with two labeled bars: 'word overlap × 0.4' and 'number overlap × 0.6'
Caption: 'real evidence lands in roughly the same place twice'
A serif landing line holds: 'a fabricated number is harder to repeat than a fabricated vibe'

beats.narration_text: Score it, classify it: high agreement, medium, or low. And raise one specific hard flag whenever a number shows up in one run but not the other at all. Run our example twice: if 34 percent shows up both times, that's real signal — a high-agreement score, something like 0.82. If the second run says 41 percent instead, with no 34 percent anywhere, that's a flag, not just a lower score — a number that only exists in one of two otherwise-similar runs is one of the strongest signals available that it was invented, not retrieved.

shot.visual_intent: The real HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW thresholds from consistency.py's _classify(), applied to the worked example twice — once agreeing (HIGH, 0.82), once diverging (LOW, 0.21) with a hard flag on the mismatched number.

show.event: Title 'Classify and Flag' writes on
A real threshold scale draws: 'LOW < 0.40 · MEDIUM 0.40–0.70 · HIGH ≥ 0.70'
Example A: 'Run 1: 34% · Run 2: 34%' seats above a green card 'HIGH agreement — 0.82'
Example B: 'Run 1: 34% · Run 2: 41%' seats above a red card 'LOW agreement — 0.21', with both numbers highlighted
A flag icon lands beside example B: 'number in one run, not the other'
A serif landing line holds: 'a fabrication can't easily fake genuine drift'

beats.act: what this doesn't prove (i) — proof vs. evidence
beats.narration_text: Here's the part that's tempting to skip, and the part that actually matters most. None of these three mechanisms proves the agent reasoned correctly. High consistency is weak positive evidence, not a guarantee — two runs can agree with each other while both being confidently, identically wrong. A model doesn't need real evidence to be consistent; it just needs to draw on the same internalized pattern twice. Verification only checks that a number exists somewhere in the cited source — it can't confirm the agent's causal story about what that number means. And a citation coming back unattainable tells you nothing either way.

shot.visual_intent: The word PROOF is struck through and replaced with EVIDENCE — the falsifiability turn of the whole episode, landing before any recap.

show.event: The word 'PROOF' writes on, large, center screen
A red strike line draws across it
'EVIDENCE' fades in beside/beneath the struck word
A line seats below: 'high consistency = weak positive evidence'
A second line seats beneath: 'two runs can agree while both are confidently wrong'
A third line: 'unattainable tells you nothing either way'
Everything but EVIDENCE fades, holding as the landing frame

beats.act: what this doesn't prove (ii) — good at catching, not proving
beats.narration_text: What these mechanisms are actually good at is the other direction: catching disagreement, catching absence, catching drift. Low consistency is strong negative evidence — it's very hard to accidentally look inconsistent while being right. A citation where the source is real but the claimed number simply isn't there is a real, structural problem, full stop. These tools reliably catch when something is wrong. They were never built to certify that something is right — treating them as if they could just relocates the trust problem one layer down instead of solving it.

shot.visual_intent: The falsifiability/stress-test beat: a two-column card names exactly what these mechanisms are strong at and exactly what they cannot claim, so the episode never overclaims its own tools.

show.event: Title 'What These Tools Are Built For' writes on
A two-column card draws: left header 'Good at catching' listing fabrication / drift / absent evidence; right header 'Cannot prove' listing correct causal reasoning / sound judgment
Left column items check off one at a time in the accent color
Right column items get a dash, not a check, in soft grey
Caption beneath the card: 'checked ≠ correct'
A serif landing line holds: 'catching wrong is not the same as certifying right'

beats.narration_text: So here's what actually holds up. One: don't grade the story, grade the claims — break reasoning into small, checkable pieces before you evaluate any of it. Two: check what can be checked against the outside world, and log honestly when something can't be checked at all, instead of quietly assuming pass. Three: when nothing external exists to check against, make the system disagree with itself on purpose — genuine drift under repetition is one of the few signals a fabrication can't easily fake. None of these three prove truth. All three narrow what's plausible.

shot.visual_intent: The three-rule recap, each rule paired with the icon that represents its mechanism (shredder / magnifying-glass-on-filing / mirror), closing the episode's own argument before the bookends.

show.event: Title 'The Framework' writes on
Rule 1 seats left: a small shredder icon + 'grade the claims, not the story'
Rule 2 seats center: a small magnifying-glass-over-document icon + 'check what's checkable, log what isn't'
Rule 3 seats right: a small mirror icon + 'make it disagree with itself on purpose'
All three icons get a green check beneath them, aligned in a row
A serif footnote holds beneath the row: 'none of these prove truth. all three narrow what's plausible.'

beats.narration_text: So: don't grade the story, grade the claims. Check what can be checked against the outside world, and log it honestly when something can't be. And when nothing external exists to check, make the system disagree with itself on purpose — because genuine drift is one of the few things a fabrication can't fake. None of this proves truth. All of it narrows what's plausible.

props.artifactHeading: Grade the Claims, Not the Story

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take a real reasoning trace — one of your own agent's outputs, or a sample one. First, tag it by hand: mark every citation, every number, every hedge word, every causal claim. Then pick one citation and actually go check it against the real source — did the number show up? If there's no external source to check, run the same prompt twice and see whether the specific numbers survive the second pass.

props.command: Can I actually verify one claim my own agent made?
output: Tag a real trace: citation, number, hedge, causal claim
Pick one citation — actually check it against the source
No source? Run it twice and watch the numbers for drift

beats.narration_text: That gap — between checking and proving — is exactly where the next problem lives: what happens when you've got more than one agent, and they don't agree at all. Signing off — Divij Pawar.

props.title: How Do You Know It Worked?
props.subline: Grade the claims. Check what's checkable. Probe the rest.
